Q: I want to inspect kernel hardware operations A:

A good starting point is strace. It lets you see when a program makes system calls and enters kernel mode. If you want to go deeper, tools like perf or ftrace can show what the kernel is doing after the syscall. I'd start with strace first since it's much easier to understand before moving on to lower-level tracing tools.

Q: How to share common templates across groups in GitLab A:

I am unsure if this is still a concern for you but while digging around for a solution I found this article that is what I am using to guide my way through the problem.

TL;DR

  1. Create a project for storing your template
  2. Add your template yaml
  3. Reference it in your project .gitlab-ci.yaml files with an include stanza
include:
  - project: 'full/path/to/project'  
    ref: 'master'
    file: '<file_name>.yml'

The project path is as you would find it in your URL when look at the project in GitLab.

Q: How to retrieve a variable from another threading.Thread? A:

Variable data_load is created in thread when it runs data_load = ...

If thread is slow then python may try to run Label(..., text=data_load) before thread creates this variable.
Simple method for this problem: create variable with some default value at start in main code.

data_load = ""

threading.Thread(target=get_data_loop).start()

# ...

data_label = tk.Label(root, text=data_load)

But code has other problem: assigning new value to data_load will not update text in Label.

It may need to use root.after(milliseconds, function) to execute (every few milliseconds) function which will use data_label to update text in Label.

def update_label():

    data_label["text"] = data_load

    root.after(200, update_label)  # repeate after 200ms (0.2s)

Full working code.

I used time to generate new data - so everyone can simply copy and test it.

import tkinter as tk
import threading
import time


def get_data_loop():
    global data_load  # PEP8: all `global` at the beginning of function

    while True:
        try:
            # data = open("data.txt", "r")
            # data_load = data.readline()  # s()[0]
            # data.close()
            time.sleep(1)  # reduce CPU usage
            data_load = time.strftime("%H:%M:%S")
        except Exception as ex:
            print("Exception:", ex)


def update_label():
    data_label["text"] = data_load

    root.after(200, update_label)  # repeate after 200ms (0.2s)


# --- main ---

data_load = ""

threading.Thread(target=get_data_loop).start()

root = tk.Tk()
root.geometry("300x300")

data_label = tk.Label(root, text=data_load)
data_label.pack()

update_label()  # run first time at once
# root.after(200, update_label)  # run first time after 200ms

root.mainloop()

It is preferred to use queue.Queue` because it is thread-safe.

You can see it in question: python - tkinter thread communication - Stack Overflow

If your function is fast (and it doesn't block tkinter to update GUI) then maybe you should read file directly with root.after() instead of using thread and while.

import tkinter as tk
import time


def update_label():
    try:
        # data = open("data.txt", "r")
        # data_load = data.readline()  # s()[0]
        # data.close()
        time.sleep(1)  # reduce CPU usage
        data_load = time.strftime("%H:%M:%S")
    except Exception as ex:
        print("Exception:", ex)

    data_label["text"] = data_load

    root.after(200, update_label)  # repeat after 200ms (0.2s)


# --- main ---

data_load = ""

root = tk.Tk()
root.geometry("300x300")

data_label = tk.Label(root, text=data_load)
data_label.pack()

update_label()  # run first time at once
# root.after(200, update_label)   # run first time after 200ms (0.2s)

root.mainloop()
